To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the seasonal Kendall test is a robust test for trend in monthly water quality data and the seasonal Kendall slope estimate is an appropriate estimator of trend magnitude in monthly water quality time series.

(1) The seasonal Kendall test is robust in the face of serial correlation and is the best nonparametric test of trend available; (2) The seasonal Kendall slope estimator is an unbiased and precise estimator of the slope magnitude of a linear trend; (3) Flow adjusted concentrations can be used to identify trends in water quality independent of discharge.

the seasonal Kendall test is robust in comparison with parametric alternatives for trend detection, the seasonal Kendall estimator has higher precision in skewed data, and the flow adjusted concentration method provides an effective means of identifying flow relatedness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of trend detection in monthly water quality time series.

the development of statistical methods for the analysis of water-quality time series that are suitable for the exploratory examination of trends in the face of nonnormality, seasonality, serial correlation, and missing or censored data.
the development of techniques that are appropriate for the analysis of monthly water-quality data sets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the techniques described here are useful for exploratory analysis of trend in monthly water quality data and are robust in the face of many of the complications that are inherent in such data.
the techniques described are useful for exploratory analysis of water quality data, but that the conclusions drawn must be considered tentative until corroborated by more detailed analysis.

these procedures provide a means for detecting trends in water quality data that are not subject to the problems of serial correlation, seasonality, skew, and missing values that have been the focus of much of the recent literature on trend analysis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the techniques described here are useful for the exploratory study of trends in monthly water quality data and that, in general, the techniques are more robust than alternatives.

the seasonal Kendall test is a robust test for trend, the seasonal Kendall test slope estimator is an unbiased estimator with high precision for normal data and moderate precision for highly skewed data, and the flow adjusted concentration test is an effective means of identifying trends that are not artifacts of the flow record.

the nonparametric techniques are robust in the face of seasonality, missing observations, and values reported as 'below the limit of detection', while the regression techniques are more precise when the data are approximately normal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the seasonal Kendall test is a powerful and flexible tool for the detection and analysis of monotonic trends in water quality time series.
nonparametric methods are useful in the analysis of water-quality trends in the presence of seasonality, serial correlation, and other data complications.
the seasonal Kendall test is a powerful tool in the exploratory analysis and trend identification of monthly water quality time series.
